claim: Intracranial EEG was recorded from 11 patients with pharmaco-resistant epilepsy at the Department of Epileptology, University of Bonn.
source: Intracranial EEG (iEEG) was recorded from patients suffering from pharmaco-resistant epilepsy at the Department of Epileptology, University of Bonn.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the recording method, patient population, and location.

claim: Successful associative recognition (AR) yields enhanced event-specific reinstatement of encoding patterns compared to non-associative item recognition (IR).
source: Results show that successful associative recognition (AR) yields enhanced event-specific reinstatement of encoding patterns compared to non-associative item recognition (IR).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the reinstatement analysis data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Gamma power (50–90 Hz) increases distinguish AR from IR.
source: Moreover, we found that gamma power (50–90 Hz) increases – in conjunction with alpha power (8–12 Hz) decreases not only distinguish AR from IR, but also correlate with the level of hippocampal reinstatement.
evidence: This finding is supported by time-frequency analysis data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Alpha power (8–12 Hz) decreases distinguish AR from IR.
source: Moreover, we found that gamma power (50–90 Hz) increases – in conjunction with alpha power (8–12 Hz) decreases not only distinguish AR from IR, but also correlate with the level of hippocampal reinstatement.
evidence: This finding is supported by time-frequency analysis data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Gamma power increases correlate with the level of hippocampal reinstatement.
source: Moreover, we found that gamma power (50–90 Hz) increases – in conjunction with alpha power (8–12 Hz) decreases not only distinguish AR from IR, but also correlate with the level of hippocampal reinstatement.
evidence: This correlation is demonstrated in Figure 3C showing median-split analysis of power values and reinstatement.

claim: Alpha power decreases correlate with the level of hippocampal reinstatement.
source: Moreover, we found that gamma power (50–90 Hz) increases – in conjunction with alpha power (8–12 Hz) decreases not only distinguish AR from IR, but also correlate with the level of hippocampal reinstatement.
evidence: This correlation is demonstrated in Figure 3C showing median-split analysis of power values and reinstatement.

claim: The medial temporal lobe (MTL), and the hippocampus in particular, is the key brain region supporting episodic memory.
source: Ignited by neuropsychological work and corroborated by animal models and human neuroimaging, converging evidence points to the medial temporal lobe (MTL), and the hippocampus in particular, as the key brain region supporting episodic memory (Davachi, 2006; Scoville and Milner, 1957; Squire, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Dense recurrent connections among CA3 pyramidal cells allow for auto-associative reinstatement of a previous learning pattern upon receiving a retrieval cue.
source: Specifically, dense recurrent connections among CA3 pyramidal cells are thought to allow, after a single exposure, for auto-associative reinstatement of a previous learning pattern upon receiving a retrieval cue (Marr, 1971; Rolls, 2016).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citations to computational models.

claim: Selective knock-out of the CA3 NMDA receptor results in impaired memory on a Morris water maze when only partial environmental cues are available.
source: Consistent with a role for pattern completion, selective knock-out of the CA3 NMDA receptor was shown to result in impaired memory on a Morris water maze when only partial environmental cues were available, i.e. when performance presumably relied more strongly on successful pattern completion (Nakazawa et al., 2002) (see also [Neunuebel and Knierim, 2014]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to animal research.

claim: Activation in local hippocampal cell assemblies recorded during contextual fear conditioning is reinstated during later re-exposure to the learning context.
source: Moreover, recent optical imaging and optogenetic studies in mice were able to show that activation in local hippocampal cell assemblies recorded during contextual fear conditioning is reinstated during later re-exposure to the learning context (Tayler et al., 2013) and that experimental activation of those assemblies leads to the expression of the learned behaviour (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to mouse studies.

claim: Experimental activation of hippocampal cell assemblies leads to the expression of learned behaviour.
source: Moreover, recent optical imaging and optogenetic studies in mice were able to show that activation in local hippocampal cell assemblies recorded during contextual fear conditioning is reinstated during later re-exposure to the learning context (Tayler et al., 2013) and that experimental activation of those assemblies leads to the expression of the learned behaviour (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to mouse optogenetic studies.

claim: Recent fMRI studies have furnished evidence for pattern reinstatement in category-specific neocortical brain regions during successful recollection.
source: Indeed, using this analytical approach, a series of recent fMRI studies have furnished evidence for pattern reinstatement in category-specific neocortical brain regions during successful recollection (Bosch et al., 2014; Horner et al., 2015; Ritchey et al., 2012; Staresina et al., 2012b; Tompary et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to fMRI studies.

claim: High-frequency gamma power increases in the hippocampus have consistently been related to successful memory encoding and retrieval.
source: For instance, high-frequency gamma power increases in the hippocampus have consistently been related to successful memory encoding and retrieval (Burke et al., 2014; Hanslmayr et al., 2016), which raises the possibility that gamma power (and/or power changes in other frequencies) might be directly linked to hippocampal pattern completion.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The average hit rate was 0.76 (±0.04).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from Table 1.

claim: The average correct rejection rate was 0.79 (±0.05).
source: correct rejection	0.79 (0.05)
evidence: This is a behavioral result from Table 1.

claim: Response latencies were significantly shorter for AR compared to IR (1.91 s (±0.13 s) vs. 2.14 s (±0.12 s), t(10) = 2.88, P = 0.016).
source: Response latencies were significantly shorter for AR compared to IR (1.91 s (±0.13 s) vs. 2.14 s (±0.12 s), t(10) = 2.88, P = 0.016).
evidence: This is a behavioral result with statistical test.

claim: After artefact rejection, the AR condition contained an average of 87 trials (range 43–141) and the IR condition contained an average of 81 trials (range 32–137) with no significant difference (t(10) = 0.30, P = 0.767).
source: After artefact rejection, the AR condition contained an average of 87 trials (range 43–141) and the IR condition contained an average of 81 trials (range 32–137) (t(10) = 0.30, P = 0.767).
evidence: This describes the trial counts after preprocessing.

claim: Encoding patterns from ~0.5 to 1 s are reliably reinstated from ~1 to 1.5 s during successful AR.
source: Results show that encoding patterns from ~0.5 to 1 s are reliably reinstated from ~1 to 1.5 s during successful AR.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2C showing the conjunction analysis.

claim: A relative gamma power (~50–90 Hz) increase for AR occurs from ~0.5 to 1.3 s.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, results revealed two clusters that showed differential effects for AR vs. IR: A relative gamma power (~50–90 Hz) increase for AR from ~0.5 to 1.3 s, followed by a relative alpha power (~8–12 Hz) increase for IR from ~1 to 2 s.
evidence: This is shown in the time-frequency analysis in Figure 3A.

claim: A relative alpha power (~8–12 Hz) increase for IR occurs from ~1 to 2 s.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, results revealed two clusters that showed differential effects for AR vs. IR: A relative gamma power (~50–90 Hz) increase for AR from ~0.5 to 1.3 s, followed by a relative alpha power (~8–12 Hz) increase for IR from ~1 to 2 s.
evidence: This is shown in the time-frequency analysis in Figure 3A.

claim: Gamma power from ~0.5 to 1.3 s correlated negatively with alpha power from ~1 to 2 s both on a trial-by-trial level and across participants.
source: Interestingly, we found that gamma power from ~0.5 to 1.3 s correlated negatively with alpha power from ~1 to 2 s both on a trial-by-trial level and across participants (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This correlation is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: AR trials with greater gamma power yielded greater reinstatement than AR trials with lower gamma power (0.050 vs. 031; t(10) = 2.82, P = 0.018).
source: Follow-up pairwise t-tests revealed that while AR trials with greater gamma power yielded greater reinstatement than AR trials with lower gamma power (0.050 vs. 031; t(10) = 2.82, P = 0.018), alpha power showed a trend in the opposite direction (0.031 vs 0.052; t(10) = 1.95, P = 0.079).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the median-split analysis.

claim: Alpha power showed a trend where lower alpha power was associated with greater reinstatement (0.031 vs 0.052; t(10) = 1.95, P = 0.079).
source: Follow-up pairwise t-tests revealed that while AR trials with greater gamma power yielded greater reinstatement than AR trials with lower gamma power (0.050 vs. 031; t(10) = 2.82, P = 0.018), alpha power showed a trend in the opposite direction (0.031 vs 0.052; t(10) = 1.95, P = 0.079).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the median-split analysis showing a trend.

claim: There was a significant interaction of relative power (high, low) x frequency band (gamma, alpha) on reinstatement values (F(1,10) = 12.16, P = 0.006).
source: Indeed, results revealed a significant interaction of relative power (high, low) x frequency band (gamma, alpha) on reinstatement values (F(1,10) = 12.16, P = 0.006) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ANOVA analysis.

claim: No single frequency band alone was sufficient to drive reinstatement across all participants and trials.
source: Results (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) showed that while the reinstatement effects prevailed when excluding any particular frequency band, no single band alone was sufficient to drive reinstatement across all participants and trials, suggesting that event-specific hippocampal reinstatement capitalizes on the rich information profile carried by a wider range of frequencies.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the frequency band exclusion analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Event-specific hippocampal reinstatement capitalizes on the rich information profile carried by a wider range of frequencies.
source: Results (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) showed that while the reinstatement effects prevailed when excluding any particular frequency band, no single band alone was sufficient to drive reinstatement across all participants and trials, suggesting that event-specific hippocampal reinstatement capitalizes on the rich information profile carried by a wider range of frequencies.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the frequency band analysis.

claim: Reinstatement reaches its maximum ~0.5 s prior to the behavioural response.
source: More importantly, the response-locked analysis of our data (Figure 4A–B) shows that reinstatement reaches its maximum ~0.5 s prior to the behavioural response, which is in good agreement with a recent report showing the peak cortical reinstatement during paired-associate word recall in the same time window via electrocorticography (Yaffe et al., 2014).
evidence: This is shown in the response-locked analysis in Figure 4.

claim: The increase in gamma power prior to the behavioural response was highly specific to AR trials and did not distinguish further between IR, M and CR trials.
source: Contrary to this prediction and as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2, the increase in gamma power prior to the behavioural response was highly specific to AR trials and did not distinguish further between IR, M and CR trials.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the omnibus ANOVA analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: AR trials were accompanied by significantly greater gamma power than all other conditions (all t(10) > 2.63, P<0.026).
source: Pairwise comparisons showed that AR trials were accompanied by significantly greater gamma power than all other conditions (all t(10) > 2.63, P<0.026), with no difference across IR, M and CR trials (all t(10) < 1.53, P>0.159.
evidence: This is shown in the bar graph in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was no difference in gamma power across IR, M and CR trials (all t(10) < 1.53, P>0.159).
source: Pairwise comparisons showed that AR trials were accompanied by significantly greater gamma power than all other conditions (all t(10) > 2.63, P<0.026), with no difference across IR, M and CR trials (all t(10) < 1.53, P>0.159.
evidence: This is shown in the bar graph in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Hippocampal gamma power selectively supports recollection-based associative recognition.
source: To the extent that our AR condition is particularly sensitive to recollection, this finding points, at least in the current paradigm, to a selective role of hippocampal gamma power in recollection-based associative recognition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of gamma power differences across conditions.

claim: Increased gamma power during memory retrieval may reflect the temporal alignment (synchronization) of target pyramidal cells.
source: Hence, increased gamma power during memory retrieval may first and foremost reflect the temporal alignment (synchronization) of target pyramidal cells, which may co-occur with a net firing rate decrease (e.g., [Axmacher et al., 2008]).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on cited literature about inhibitory interneuron networks.

claim: The observed gamma power increase for AR vs. IR trials may correspond to a selective recruitment mechanism, prioritizing neurons that represent the target association whilst de-prioritizing neurons representing non-relevant information.
source: Accordingly, one tentative interpretation is that the observed gamma power increase for AR vs. IR trials in our study may correspond to a selective recruitment mechanism, prioritizing neurons that represent the target association whilst de-prioritizing neurons representing non-relevant information.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the gamma power findings.

claim: Alpha-band oscillations have traditionally been linked to idling states or the suppression of activity within particular functional networks in sensory cortices.
source: Alpha-band oscillations have traditionally been linked to idling states or the suppression of activity within particular functional networks in sensory cortices (Berger, 1929; Jensen et al., 2012; Klimesch, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The relative increase of alpha power for IR may reflect disengagement of hippocampal retrieval operations upon failure to surpass a certain recollection threshold.
source: Applied to our current results, the relative increase of alpha power for IR (Figure 3) may hence reflect disengagement of hippocampal retrieval operations upon failure to surpass a certain recollection threshold.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the alpha power findings.

claim: Neural desynchronization in alpha/beta bands (expressed in power decreases) reflects an increase in sensory information content.
source: Another recent account proposes that neural desynchronization in alpha/beta bands (expressed in power decreases) reflects an increase in sensory information content (Hanslmayr et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The relative decrease in alpha power for AR may reflect an increase in information (i.e. the target association) resulting from effective retrieval operations.
source: In that sense, the relative decrease for AR may reflect an increase in information (i.e. the target association) resulting from effective retrieval operations.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the information content account.

claim: There is a direct relationship between associative retrieval processes as reflected by the power in the gamma band and the amount of mnemonic information available as inversely reflected by the power in the alpha band.
source: One tentative interpretation is therefore towards a direct relationship between (i) associative retrieval processes as reflected by the power in the gamma band and (ii) the amount of mnemonic information available as inversely reflected by the power in the alpha band.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the negative correlation between gamma and alpha power.

claim: The same alpha band cluster (8–12 Hz) showed greater power for IR relative to AR during encoding, with a markedly earlier timing of this effect than during retrieval (~0.2 to 0.9 s during encoding vs. ~1 to 2 s during retrieval).
source: Interestingly, when contrasting AR with IR trials during encoding, the same alpha band cluster (8–12 Hz) emerged to show greater power for IR relative to AR, but critically with a markedly earlier timing of this effect than during retrieval (~0.2 to 0.9 s during encoding vs. ~1 to 2 s during retrieval; Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in the encoding analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Depth electrodes were implanted stereotactically, either via the occipital lobe along the longitudinal axis of the hippocampus or laterally via the temporal lobe.
source: Depth electrodes were implanted stereotactically, either via the occipital lobe along the longitudinal axis of the hippocampus or laterally via the temporal lobe, during presurgical evaluation (the seizure onset zone could not be precisely determined with noninvasive methods).
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure for electrode implantation.

claim: Depth electroencephalograms were referenced to linked mastoids and recorded with a sampling rate of 1 kHz.
source: Depth electroencephalograms were referenced to linked mastoids and recorded with a sampling rate of 1 kHz (bandpass filter: 0.01 Hz (6 dB per octave) to 300 Hz (12 dB per octave)).
evidence: This describes the recording parameters.

claim: A total of 15 patients participated in the study, out of which 4 were excluded from subsequent analyses.
source: A total of 15 patients participated in the study, out of which 4 were excluded from subsequent analyses.
evidence: This describes the participant sample.

claim: Of the remaining 11 participants, 6 were female and 5 were male with a mean age of 34 years (range: 23–51).
source: Of the remaining 11 participants, 6 were female and 5 were male. Mean age was 34 years (range: 23–51).
evidence: This describes the demographic characteristics of the final sample.

claim: Clinical evaluation revealed a unilateral epileptic focus in the left hemisphere of 8 patients and in the right hemisphere hippocampus of 2 patients.
source: Clinical evaluation revealed a unilateral epileptic focus in the left hemisphere of 8 patients (7 in the hippocampus, 1 in the anterior temporal lobe) and in the right hemisphere hippocampus of 2 patients.
evidence: This describes the clinical characteristics of the patient sample.

claim: Only data from the hemisphere contralateral to the seizure onset zone were included.
source: Only data from the hemisphere contralateral to the seizure onset zone were included.
evidence: This describes the data selection criterion.

claim: The sample consisted of 8 right hemisphere and 3 left hemisphere hippocampal datasets.
source: Thus, our sample consisted of 8 right hemisphere and 3 left hemisphere hippocampal datasets.
evidence: This describes the final composition of the dataset.

claim: During encoding, participants were presented with a German noun paired during colour runs with the colour blue or red, and during scene runs with the image of an indoor or an outdoor scene.
source: During encoding, participants were presented with a German noun paired during colour runs with the colour blue or red, and during scene runs with the image of an indoor or an outdoor scene (office or nature).
evidence: This describes the experimental stimuli.

claim: The encoding task was to vividly imagine the referent of the noun in the given colour/scene and to rate the plausibility of that image as plausible or implausible.
source: The encoding task was to vividly imagine the referent of the noun in the given colour/scene and to rate the plausibility of that image as plausible or implausible.
evidence: This describes the encoding task.

claim: Participants were given 3 s to make their plausibility judgment.
source: Participants were given 3 s to make their plausibility judgment.
evidence: This describes the timing constraint for the encoding task.

claim: During retrieval, participants were presented with 75 trials including the 50 previously seen words along with 25 novel words.
source: During retrieval, participants were presented with 75 trials including the 50 previously seen words along with 25 novel words.
evidence: This describes the retrieval test composition.

claim: The retrieval task was to indicate, with a single button press, whether the word was new, whether it was old but the target association could not be retrieved ('?' responses), or whether the word was old and the target association was also remembered.
source: The task was to indicate, with a single button press, whether the word was new, whether it was old but the target association could not be retrieved ('?' responses), or whether the word was old and the target association was also remembered.
evidence: This describes the retrieval task.

claim: Responses were given in a self-paced manner, with an upper time limit of 5 s.
source: Responses were given in a self-paced manner, with an upper time limit of 5 s.
evidence: This describes the timing constraint for the retrieval task.

claim: Eight participants completed all six runs and three participants completed five runs.
source: Eight participants completed all six runs and three participants completed five runs.
evidence: This describes the number of experimental runs completed.

claim: For group-level analyses, one hippocampal depth electrode contact per participant was selected based on anatomical and functional criteria.
source: For group-level analyses, we selected one hippocampal depth electrode contact per participant based on anatomical and functional criteria.
evidence: This describes the electrode selection procedure.

claim: Anterior hippocampal electrodes were favoured because associative memory effects have been reliably observed in this region.
source: Anterior hippocampal electrodes were favoured because associative memory effects have been reliably observed in this region (for review, see [Davachi, 2006]) and recent theoretical accounts postulate a specific role of the anterior hippocampus in pattern completion (whereas the posterior hippocampus might be biased towards pattern separation) (Poppenk et al., 2013).
evidence: This is justified by citations to prior research.

claim: Recent theoretical accounts postulate a specific role of the anterior hippocampus in pattern completion (whereas the posterior hippocampus might be biased towards pattern separation).
source: Anterior hippocampal electrodes were favoured because associative memory effects have been reliably observed in this region (for review, see [Davachi, 2006]) and recent theoretical accounts postulate a specific role of the anterior hippocampus in pattern completion (whereas the posterior hippocampus might be biased towards pattern separation) (Poppenk et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: Across participants, an average of 12% of all trials (range: 7%–21%) were excluded due to artifacts.
source: Across participants, an average of 12% of all trials (range: 7%–21%) were thus excluded.
evidence: This describes the proportion of trials excluded during preprocessing.

claim: For lower frequencies (2–29 Hz, 1-Hz steps), the window length was set to five cycles of a given frequency, and the windowed data segments were multiplied with a Hanning taper before Fourier analysis.
source: For a lower frequency range (2–29 Hz, 1-Hz steps), the window length was set to five cycles of a given frequency (for example, 500 ms for 10 Hz; 250 ms for 20 Hz), and the windowed data segments were multiplied with a Hanning taper before Fourier analysis.
evidence: This describes the time-frequency analysis parameters for lower frequencies.

claim: For higher frequencies (30–100 Hz, 5-Hz steps), multitapering was applied using a fixed window length of 400 ms and seven orthogonal Slepian tapers (resulting in spectral smoothing of ~±10Hz).
source: For higher frequencies (30–100 Hz, 5-Hz steps), we applied multitapering, using a fixed window length of 400 ms and seven orthogonal Slepian tapers (resulting in spectral smoothing of ~±10Hz) (this approach was adopted from [Jokisch and Jensen, 2007]).
evidence: This describes the time-frequency analysis parameters for higher frequencies.

claim: The field potential picked up by a single intracranial macro-electrode reflects contributions from all active cellular processes within the underlying volume of brain tissue.
source: Moreover, as comprehensively reviewed by Buzsaki and colleagues (Buzsáki et al., 2012), the field potential picked up by a single intracranial macro-electrode reflects contributions from all active cellular processes within the underlying volume of brain tissue (including synaptic activity, action potentials, fluctuations in glia etc.).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: The time-frequency-decomposed signal might be particularly well suited to capture local hippocampal pattern completion processes.
source: As amplitude and frequency of the recorded field potential depend on the proportional contribution of these multiple sources, the time-frequency-decomposed signal might be particularly well suited to capture local hippocampal pattern completion processes in our study (i.e. firing patterns of distributed neurons bias the measured field potentials differentially; see also [Agarwal et al., 2014], although that study used even finer-grained micro-electrode field recordings from the rodent hippocampus).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation.

claim: A non-parametric cluster-based permutation procedure was used for statistical comparisons of reinstatement maps or power maps.
source: For statistical comparisons of reinstatement maps or power maps, we used a non-parametric cluster-based permutation procedure implemented in FieldTrip (Maris and Oostenveld, 2007).
evidence: This describes the statistical method used.

claim: The alpha level was set to 5% across all analyses.
source: The alpha level was set to 5% across all analyses, and parametric t tests were always two-tailed.
evidence: This describes the statistical threshold used.

claim: The same pattern of results was observed when using only the 43 frequency values at a given time point as the representational pattern.
source: In the first variant, we used only the 43 frequency values at a given time point as the representational pattern, i.e. without concatenating or averaging across multiple time points. All pairwise comparisons (AR vs. IR stimulus-locked, AR vs. AR surrogate stimulus-locked, AR vs. IR response-locked, AR vs. AR surrogate response-locked) were significant (all t(10) > 2.66, P<0.024).
evidence: This demonstrates robustness of the reinstatement findings to different analysis parameters.

claim: The same pattern of results was observed when extending the time window from 400 ms to 500 ms.
source: Next, we extended our time window from 400 ms to 500 ms, with the representational pattern thus containing 43 x 51 power values. Again, all four pairwise comparisons were significant (all t(10) > 2.90, P<0.017).
evidence: This demonstrates robustness of the reinstatement findings to different time window sizes.

claim: The same pattern of results was observed when averaging the power values across 500 ms.
source: Finally, to match the above-mentioned study (Yaffe et al., 2014) as closely as possible, we averaged the power values across those 500 ms, with the representational pattern thus containing 43 power values (one value integrating power across 500 ms at each frequency). As before, all four pairwise comparisons were significant (all t(10) > 2.37, P<0.040).
evidence: This demonstrates robustness of the reinstatement findings to temporal averaging.

claim: Pattern completion is the central mechanism underlying successful recollection according to computational models.
source: Based on the physiological properties of the hippocampal CA3 subregion, computational models have proposed 'pattern completion' as the central mechanism underlying successful recollection.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on computational models.

claim: Direct empirical evidence for pattern completion in the human hippocampus has been lacking prior to this study.
source: With these basic criteria in mind, direct empirical evidence for pattern completion in the human hippocampus has thus far been lacking.
evidence: This is a claim about the state of the literature prior to the current study.

claim: Previous fMRI studies did not show hippocampal reinstatement after single exposure and its relation to successful vs. unsuccessful recollection.
source: However, hippocampal reinstatement after single exposure and its relation to successful vs. unsuccessful recollection has not been investigated in those studies.
evidence: This is a claim about limitations of prior fMRI studies.

claim: The hippocampus has been found to co-vary with reinstatement in cortical regions in terms of BOLD activation levels in fMRI studies.
source: Interestingly, in those studies, despite not exhibiting reinstatement itself, the hippocampus has been found to co-vary with reinstatement in cortical regions in terms of BOLD activation levels (see also [Gordon et al., 2014]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies.

claim: The hippocampus orchestrates cortical reinstatement.
source: While consistent with a role of the hippocampus in orchestrating cortical reinstatement (Staresina et al., 2013a; Teyler and DiScenna, 1986), there must be – despite sparse coding and possible remapping of cells (Colgin et al., 2008; Quiroga et al., 2008) - some representational overlap between an event's retrieval pattern and its designated encoding pattern in the hippocampus in order to ignite the recollection process.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There must be some representational overlap between an event's retrieval pattern and its designated encoding pattern in the hippocampus in order to ignite the recollection process.
source: While consistent with a role of the hippocampus in orchestrating cortical reinstatement (Staresina et al., 2013a; Teyler and DiScenna, 1986), there must be – despite sparse coding and possible remapping of cells (Colgin et al., 2008; Quiroga et al., 2008) - some representational overlap between an event's retrieval pattern and its designated encoding pattern in the hippocampus in order to ignite the recollection process.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the necessity of pattern overlap for recollection.

claim: The comparison with IR trials rules out that reinstatement during AR merely reflects seeing the same noun on the screen.
source: Note that the comparison with IR trials also rules out that reinstatement during AR merely reflects seeing the same noun on the screen, which would hold for both AR and IR.
evidence: This is an inference about the interpretation of the AR vs IR comparison.

claim: The surrogate analysis controls for conceivably non-specific features shared across AR trials.
source: Likewise, our stringent surrogate analysis controls for conceivably non-specific features shared across AR trials (e.g., greater signal-to-noise ratios), even when the same target association was retrieved.
evidence: This is an inference about what the surrogate analysis controls for.

claim: The results reflect reinstatement of the trial-unique combination of noun, associative detail and potentially other event-specific contextual variables.
source: These controls suggest that our results indeed reflect reinstatement of the trial-unique combination of noun, associative detail and potentially other event-specific contextual variables (internal or external and akin to 'holistic pattern completion processes' identified by Horner and colleagues [Horner et al., 2015; Horner and Burgess, 2014]).
evidence: This is an inference about what the reinstatement represents, supported by citation.

claim: Earlier encoding patterns are reinstated later during retrieval.
source: In the stimulus-locked analysis (Figure 2), the peak effect entailed ~0.5–1 s encoding patterns being reinstated from 1–1.5 s at retrieval. While also showing that earlier encoding patterns are reinstated later during retrieval, the corresponding time windows were considerably earlier in a recent study assessing memory reinstatement via MEG (where encoding representations around 180 ms were reinstated at ~500 ms at retrieval; [Jafarpour et al., 2014]).
evidence: This is an observation from the data, compared with a cited MEG study.

claim: The peak cortical reinstatement during paired-associate word recall occurs ~0.5 s prior to the behavioural response.
source: More importantly, the response-locked analysis of our data (Figure 4A–B) shows that reinstatement reaches its maximum ~0.5 s prior to the behavioural response, which is in good agreement with a recent report showing the peak cortical reinstatement during paired-associate word recall in the same time window via electrocorticography (Yaffe et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an electrocorticography study.

claim: Hippocampal gamma power not only distinguishes successful from unsuccessful associative recognition, but also correlates with the level of reinstatement within the AR condition.
source: Here, we were able to show that hippocampal gamma power not only distinguishes successful from unsuccessful associative recognition, but also - within the AR condition - trials of higher vs. lower levels of reinstatement (Figure 3C), extending the link between hippocampal gamma power and episodic memory from solely behavioural to neurophysiological measures of recollection.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: A recent iEEG study challenges the notion that hippocampal gamma power selectively supports episodic recollection.
source: That said, a recent iEEG study challenges the notion that hippocampal gamma power selectively supports episodic recollection (Merkow et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Merkow et al. (2015) found that hippocampal gamma power not only supported recollection, but also scaled with different levels of familiarity-based recognition.
source: Results suggested that hippocampal gamma power not only supported recollection, but also scaled with different levels of familiarity-based recognition.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited study.

claim: Only ~50% of human hippocampal neurons respond with a firing rate increase at the second stimulus presentation compared to the first presentation in a continuous recognition task.
source: For instance, in terms of overall responses of human hippocampal neurons, only ~50% of neurons were found to respond with a firing rate increase at the second stimulus presentation compared to the first presentation in a continuous recognition task.
evidence: This is supported by citation to single-unit recording studies.

claim: Around twice as many hippocampal neurons respond to previously seen stimuli with a firing rate decrease compared to an increase.
source: In fact, around twice as many hippocampal neurons responded to previously seen stimuli with a firing rate decrease (Viskontas et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a single-unit recording study.

claim: In macaque hippocampus, almost three times the number of neurons respond with a firing rate decrease to repeated stimuli than with an increase.
source: A very similar result has been reported for recordings from macaque hippocampus (Jutras and Buffalo, 2010), with almost three times the number of neurons responding with a firing rate decrease to repeated stimuli than with an increase.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a macaque recording study.

claim: Hippocampal inhibition plays a major role in episodic memory retrieval.
source: Together, these findings raise the possibility that hippocampal inhibition plays a major role in episodic memory retrieval.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited single-unit recording studies.

claim: Inhibitory hippocampal interneuron networks, oscillating at gamma frequencies, control the firing of pyramidal cells and restrict their action potentials to specific time windows by cholinergic inputs.
source: Indeed, inhibitory hippocampal interneuron networks, oscillating at gamma frequencies, control the firing of pyramidal cells and restrict their action potentials to specific time windows by cholinergic inputs (Bartos et al., 2007; Whittington et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on interneuron networks.

claim: Alpha power decreases during successful recognition have been observed in a number of scalp EEG/MEG and electrocorticography studies.
source: Alpha power decreases during successful recognition have been observed in a number of scalp EEG/MEG and electrocorticography studies (for review, see [Hanslmayr et al., 2012]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Fairly broadband low-frequency power decreases (encompassing theta, alpha and beta frequencies) in the hippocampus support successful encoding.
source: In the hippocampus, fairly broadband low-frequency power decreases (encompassing theta, alpha and beta frequencies) in the hippocampus were found to support successful encoding (Fell et al., 2011; Sederberg et al., 2007b), but hippocampal low-frequency power decreases during successful retrieval are only rarely reported (Lega et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior hippocampal recording studies.

claim: Hippocampal low-frequency power decreases during successful retrieval are only rarely reported.
source: In the hippocampus, fairly broadband low-frequency power decreases (encompassing theta, alpha and beta frequencies) in the hippocampus were found to support successful encoding (Fell et al., 2011; Sederberg et al., 2007b), but hippocampal low-frequency power decreases during successful retrieval are only rarely reported (Lega et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a claim about the state of the literature, supported by citation.

claim: If hippocampal alpha power is related to information content, one might expect alpha differences between AR and IR to emerge earlier during encoding.
source: Pushing this idea one step further, if hippocampal alpha power is indeed related to information content, one might expect alpha differences between AR and IR to emerge earlier during encoding, in line with the notion that relatively unsuccessful encoding results from impoverished levels of incoming information.
evidence: This is a logical prediction based on the information content hypothesis.

claim: Relatively unsuccessful encoding results from impoverished levels of incoming information.
source: Pushing this idea one step further, if hippocampal alpha power is indeed related to information content, one might expect alpha differences between AR and IR to emerge earlier during encoding, in line with the notion that relatively unsuccessful encoding results from impoverished levels of incoming information.
evidence: This is a theoretical notion about encoding success.

claim: The study provides empirical evidence for a pattern completion mechanism in the human hippocampus that reinstates event-specific encoding patterns during successful recollection.
source: Using direct intracranial recordings during an associative memory paradigm, we provide empirical evidence for a pattern completion mechanism in the human hippocampus that reinstates event-specific encoding patterns during successful recollection.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Results link reinstatement to fluctuations in gamma power, hypothesized to coordinate the selection of target-relevant neurons.
source: Results further link reinstatement to fluctuations in gamma power, hypothesized to coordinate the selection of target-relevant neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion of the study with a speculative interpretation.

claim: Time-shifted hippocampal alpha power shows an inverse relationship to gamma power, potentially reflecting the amount of information relayed to and from the hippocampus during memory formation and retrieval.
source: Finally, time-shifted hippocampal alpha power showed an inverse relationship to gamma power, potentially reflecting the amount of information relayed to and from the hippocampus during memory formation and retrieval.
evidence: This is a conclusion of the study with a speculative interpretation.

claim: The average xyz coordinates of the selected hippocampal contacts were ±28, −17 and −18 mm in MNI space.
source: Based on visual identification of the contact centres, the average xyz coordinates were ±28, −17 and −18 mm.
evidence: This describes the anatomical location of the selected electrodes.

claim: Colour and scene runs alternated, with the assignment of the first run to colour or scene rotated across participants.
source: Colour and scene runs alternated, with the assignment of the first run to colour or scene rotated across participants.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Behaviour was matched between colour and scene blocks.
source: The use of colours vs. scenes was initially intended to allow investigation of differential effects across MTL cortical regions (in case a patient would have sufficient electrode coverage), but for the current purposes, we did not further differentiate across these types of associations (note also that behaviour was matched between colour and scene blocks; see Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Table 2.

claim: There was no main effect of block type on encoding responses (F(1,10) < 0.60, P>0.461).
source: As shown in Table 2, during encoding, 'plausible' and 'implausible' responses were well balanced across participants for both colour and scene blocks, with no main effect of block type, no main effect of response and no interaction between the two factors (all F(1,10) < 0.60, P>0.461).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the encoding data.

claim: There was no main effect of response type on encoding responses (F(1,10) < 0.60, P>0.461).
source: As shown in Table 2, during encoding, 'plausible' and 'implausible' responses were well balanced across participants for both colour and scene blocks, with no main effect of block type, no main effect of response and no interaction between the two factors (all F(1,10) < 0.60, P>0.461).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the encoding data.

claim: There was no interaction between block type and response type on encoding responses (F(1,10) < 0.60, P>0.461).
source: As shown in Table 2, during encoding, 'plausible' and 'implausible' responses were well balanced across participants for both colour and scene blocks, with no main effect of block type, no main effect of response and no interaction between the two factors (all F(1,10) < 0.60, P>0.461).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the encoding data.

claim: For retrieval, proportions of memory conditions were balanced across colour and scene blocks.
source: For retrieval, proportions of memory conditions were again balanced across colour and scene blocks, with an average of 51% (±6%) AR trials vs. 49% (±6%) IR trials for colour blocks and an average of 52% (±5%) AR trials vs. 48% (±5%) IR trials for scene blocks, without a main effect of condition nor a condition x block type interaction (both F(1,10) < 0.15, P>0.706).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the retrieval data.

claim: There was no main effect of condition on retrieval proportions across block types (F(1,10) < 0.15, P>0.706).
source: For retrieval, proportions of memory conditions were again balanced across colour and scene blocks, with an average of 51% (±6%) AR trials vs. 49% (±6%) IR trials for colour blocks and an average of 52% (±5%) AR trials vs. 48% (±5%) IR trials for scene blocks, without a main effect of condition nor a condition x block type interaction (both F(1,10) < 0.15, P>0.706).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the retrieval data.

claim: There was no condition x block type interaction on retrieval proportions (F(1,10) < 0.15, P>0.706).
source: For retrieval, proportions of memory conditions were again balanced across colour and scene blocks, with an average of 51% (±6%) AR trials vs. 49% (±6%) IR trials for colour blocks and an average of 52% (±5%) AR trials vs. 48% (±5%) IR trials for scene blocks, without a main effect of condition nor a condition x block type interaction (both F(1,10) < 0.15, P>0.706).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the retrieval data.

claim: There was only a main effect of Memory on response latencies (F(1,10) = 6.75, P = 0.027), without a Category main effect (F(1,10) = 1.54, P = 0.243) or a Category x Memory interaction (F(1,10) = 0.68, P = 0.428).
source: Finally, when including the factor Category (colours, scenes) and Memory (AR, IR) in a repeated measures ANOVA on response latencies, there was only a main effect of Memory (F(1,10) = 6.75, P = 0.027), without a Category main effect (F(1,10) = 1.54, P = 0.243) or a Category x Memory interaction (F(1,10) = 0.68, P = 0.428).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the response latency analysis.

claim: A representational pattern was defined as a 400 ms time window (10 ms temporal resolution) including the proportional power changes from 2 to 100 Hz relative to a 500 ms prestimulus baseline window.
source: First, a representational pattern was defined as a 400 ms time window (10 ms temporal resolution) including the proportional power changes from 2 to 100 Hz (1-Hz steps from 2–29 Hz, 5-Hz steps from 30–100 Hz) relative to a 500 ms prestimulus baseline window (in keeping with our standard time-frequency analyses, see below).
evidence: This describes the definition of representational patterns used in the analysis.

claim: A representational pattern centred on a given time point consisted of 43 x 41 frequency values.
source: A representational pattern centred on a given time point thus consisted of 43 x 41 frequency values.
evidence: This describes the dimensionality of the representational patterns.

claim: The same results were observed when using the 43 frequencies only (i.e. not extended across time), when extending the time window from 400 ms to 500 ms, or when averaging across time points.
source: Note however that the same results were observed when using the 43 frequencies only (i.e. not extended across time), when extending the time window from 400 ms to 500 ms, or when averaging across time points (Yaffe et al., 2014); Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This demonstrates robustness of the findings to different analysis parameters.

claim: Surrogate reinstatement values for each AR trial were derived by correlating a given AR trial's retrieval patterns with the encoding patterns of all other AR trials where exactly the same target association was presented.
source: To counter this concern, we derived surrogate reinstatement values for each AR trial by correlating a given AR trial's retrieval patterns with the encoding patterns of all other AR trials where exactly the same target association was presented.
evidence: This describes the surrogate analysis procedure.

claim: The surrogate procedure controls for a potential increase in perceptual/attentional reinstatement for AR vs. IR.
source: Note that this procedure not only controls for a potential increase in perceptual/attentional reinstatement for AR vs. IR, but it further ensures event-specificity by factoring out shared similarities with all other AR trials where the same colour or scene was recollected.
evidence: This is an explanation of what the surrogate analysis controls for.

claim: The surrogate procedure ensures event-specificity by factoring out shared similarities with all other AR trials where the same colour or scene was recollected.
source: Note that this procedure not only controls for a potential increase in perceptual/attentional reinstatement for AR vs. IR, but it further ensures event-specificity by factoring out shared similarities with all other AR trials where the same colour or scene was recollected.
evidence: This is an explanation of what the surrogate analysis controls for.

claim: Reinstatement began to unfold already at ~0.5 s post stimulus onset.
source: Note also that although reinstatement reached its maximum relatively late during retrieval (~1–1.5 s), the effect began to unfold already at ~0.5 s post stimulus onset.
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 2A.

claim: Reinstatement reached its maximum relatively late during retrieval (~1–1.5 s).
source: Note also that although reinstatement reached its maximum relatively late during retrieval (~1–1.5 s), the effect began to unfold already at ~0.5 s post stimulus onset.
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 2A.

claim: There was a significant window x condition interaction for gamma power (F(1,10) = 22.15, P = 0.001) reflecting a significant increase for AR vs. IR in the post-stimulus window (t(10) = 2.65, P = 0.024) but not in the pre-stimulus baseline window (t(10) = 1.72, P>0.1).
source: First, a significant window x condition interaction for gamma power (F(1,10) = 22.15, P = 0.001) reflected a significant increase for AR vs. IR in the post-stimulus window (t(10) = 2.65, P = 0.024) but not in the pre-stimulus baseline window (t(10) = 1.72, P>0.1).
evidence: This is a statistical result confirming that gamma effects are not driven by baseline differences.

claim: There was a significant window x condition interaction for alpha power (F(1,10) = 32.62, P<0.001) reflecting a significant increase for IR vs. AR in the post-stimulus window (t(10) = 4.84, P = 0.001) but not in the pre-stimulus baseline window (t(10) = 1.38, P>0.1).
source: Likewise, a significant window x condition interaction for alpha power (F(1,10) = 32.62, P<0.001) reflected a significant increase for IR vs. AR in the post-stimulus window (t(10) = 4.84, P = 0.001) but not in the pre-stimulus baseline window (t(10) = 1.38, P>0.1) and a significant increase from baseline for IR (t(10) = 2.97, P = 0.014) but not for AR (t(10) = 0.85, P = 0.415).
evidence: This is a statistical result confirming that alpha effects are not driven by baseline differences.

claim: There was a significant increase in alpha power from baseline for IR (t(10) = 2.97, P = 0.014) but not for AR (t(10) = 0.85, P = 0.415).
source: Likewise, a significant window x condition interaction for alpha power (F(1,10) = 32.62, P<0.001) reflected a significant increase for IR vs. AR in the post-stimulus window (t(10) = 4.84, P = 0.001) but not in the pre-stimulus baseline window (t(10) = 1.38, P>0.1) and a significant increase from baseline for IR (t(10) = 2.97, P = 0.014) but not for AR (t(10) = 0.85, P = 0.415).
evidence: This is a statistical result showing differential alpha power changes from baseline.

claim: Condition differences during retrieval unfolded after stimulus onset in the paradigm.
source: These results confirm that condition differences during retrieval unfolded after stimulus onset in our paradigm.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the baseline-corrected analyses.

claim: The timing of the post-stimulus gamma and alpha differences for AR vs. IR (~0.5 to 2 s) overlaps with the time window showing pattern completion for AR trials (1 to 1.5 s).
source: Although the timing of the post-stimulus gamma and alpha differences for AR vs. IR (~0.5 to 2 s) overlaps with the time window showing pattern completion for AR trials (1 to 1.5 s), we next sought to establish a stronger link between the power effects and the reinstatement effect observed above.
evidence: This is an observation about the temporal overlap of effects.

claim: The response-locked power time courses – particularly the gamma power time course – showed a striking temporal overlap with the response-locked reinstatement time course, both showing their maximum effect size ~0.5 s prior to the memory response.
source: Critically, the response-locked power time courses – particularly the gamma power time course – showed a striking temporal overlap with the response-locked reinstatement time course, both showing their maximum effect size ~0.5 s prior to the memory response.
evidence: This is an observation from the response-locked analysis in Figure 4.

claim: The ~0.5–1 s encoding pattern was reinstated during AR trials, with a maximum between −0.8 and −0.2 s prior to the behavioural response.
source: Again, the ~0.5–1 s encoding pattern was reinstated during AR trials, with a maximum between −0.8 and −0.2 s prior to the behavioural response (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in the response-locked reinstatement analysis in Figure 4A.

claim: There was a significant gamma power (50–90 Hz) cluster from ~−0.8 to −0.2 s prior to the behavioural response in the response-locked analysis.
source: Power contrast map of AR > IR from −1 s to +0.1 s relative to the behavioural response, revealing a significant gamma power (50–90 Hz) cluster from ~−0.8 to −0.2 s during retrieval and a more sustained, narrow-band alpha power (8–12 Hz) cluster.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There was a more sustained, narrow-band alpha power (8–12 Hz) cluster in the response-locked analysis.
source: Power contrast map of AR > IR from −1 s to +0.1 s relative to the behavioural response, revealing a significant gamma power (50–90 Hz) cluster from ~−0.8 to −0.2 s during retrieval and a more sustained, narrow-band alpha power (8–12 Hz) cluster.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In three patients, clinical monitoring revealed epileptogenic activity in both hippocampi.
source: In three of these patients, clinical monitoring revealed epileptogenic activity in both hippocampi, and one patient was a non-native German speaker and had difficulties understanding the stimulus material.
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria for patients.

claim: One patient was a non-native German speaker and had difficulties understanding the stimulus material.
source: In three of these patients, clinical monitoring revealed epileptogenic activity in both hippocampi, and one patient was a non-native German speaker and had difficulties understanding the stimulus material.
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria for patients.

claim: Clinical evaluation revealed a unilateral epileptic focus in the left hemisphere of 8 patients (7 in the hippocampus, 1 in the anterior temporal lobe).
source: Clinical evaluation revealed a unilateral epileptic focus in the left hemisphere of 8 patients (7 in the hippocampus, 1 in the anterior temporal lobe) and in the right hemisphere hippocampus of 2 patients.
evidence: This describes the clinical characteristics of the patient sample.

claim: No hippocampal focus was diagnosed in 1 patient, and left hemisphere data were used based on the selection criteria.
source: No hippocampal focus was diagnosed in 1 patient, and left hemisphere data were used based on the selection criteria described below.
evidence: This describes the data selection for one patient.

claim: Each trial was preceded by a jittered intertrial interval (700–1300 ms, mean = 1000 ms) during which a fixation cross was shown in the centre of the screen.
source: Each trial was preceded by a jittered intertrial interval (700–1300 ms, mean = 1000 ms) during which a fixation cross was shown in the centre of the screen.
evidence: This describes the experimental timing.

claim: Trials terminated with the participant's button press.
source: Trials terminated with the participant's button press.
evidence: This describes the trial termination procedure.

claim: Each run lasted ~9 min.
source: Each run lasted ~9 min.
evidence: This describes the duration of experimental runs.

claim: Anterior hippocampal contacts showed reliable ERP associative recognition effects in a subset of the current sample.
source: Furthermore, anterior hippocampal contacts showed reliable ERP associative recognition effects in a subset of the current sample (Staresina et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study using a subset of the current sample.

claim: Signal quality was assessed for each channel in terms of artefactual raw trials, where artefacts were defined as time points in which both absolute amplitude and gradients exceeded the median plus 3 inter quartile ranges across −1 to +3 s around stimulus onset.
source: For initial selection purposes, signal quality was assessed for each channel in terms of artefactual raw trials, where artefacts were defined as time points in which both absolute amplitude and gradients (i.e. the difference between two adjacent time points) exceeded the median plus 3 inter quartile ranges across −1 to +3 s around stimulus onset.
evidence: This describes the artifact detection procedure.

claim: This artifact detection procedure proved sensitive to detecting epileptogenic activation.
source: This procedure proved sensitive to detecting epileptogenic activation.
evidence: This is a statement about the effectiveness of the artifact detection method.

claim: The lateral implantation scheme (n=4) typically includes depth electrodes with two closely spaced contacts in the anterior hippocampus.
source: The lateral implantation scheme (n=4) typically includes depth electrodes with two closely spaced contacts in the anterior hippocampus, and provided that both contacts were located within the hippocampus, the contact with higher signal quality was selected.
evidence: This describes the electrode configuration for lateral implantations.

claim: The longitudinal implantation scheme (n=7) typically contains depth electrodes with 10 evenly spaced contacts, with the anterior ~2–4 contacts located in peri/entorhinal cortex and the remaining ~6–8 contacts spanning anterior to posterior hippocampus.
source: The longitudinal implantation scheme (n=7) typically contains depth electrodes with 10 evenly spaced contacts, with the anterior ~2–4 contacts located in peri/entorhinal cortex and the remaining ~6–8 contacts spanning anterior to posterior hippocampus (see Figure 1B for an example).
evidence: This describes the electrode configuration for longitudinal implantations.

claim: Pairwise channel coherence (2–10 Hz) was calculated to reveal functional transitions from rhinal cortex to anterior hippocampus and from anterior hippocampus to posterior hippocampus.
source: To complement the anatomical demarcation of rhinal cortex, anterior hippocampus and posterior hippocampus based on the post-implantation MRI, we calculated the pairwise channel coherence (2–10 Hz) to reveal functional transitions from rhinal cortex to anterior hippocampus and from anterior hippocampus to posterior hippocampus ([Mormann et al., 2008]; for more details, see [Staresina et al., 2012a]).
evidence: This describes the functional localization method, supported by citations.

claim: In one patient, the delineation between rhinal cortex and anterior hippocampus was less clear, and a contact in the posterior hippocampus was selected for that patient.
source: In one patient, the delineation between rhinal cortex and anterior hippocampus was less clear, and to avoid ambiguities about rhinal vs. hippocampal signal generators, we selected a contact in the posterior hippocampus for that patient.
evidence: This describes an exception in the electrode selection procedure.

claim: Results remained unchanged when excluding the patient with a posterior hippocampus contact from the analyses.
source: Results remained unchanged, however, when excluding that patient from the analyses.
evidence: This demonstrates robustness of the findings.

claim: Data processing was performed with FieldTrip and standard MATLAB functions.
source: Data processing was performed with FieldTrip (Oostenveld et al., 2010) and standard MATLAB functions.
evidence: This describes the software used for data analysis.

claim: Artifact rejection was performed on trial epochs from −1 to +3 s time locked to stimulus onset.
source: Artifact rejection was performed on trial epochs from −1 to +3 s time locked to stimulus onset.
evidence: This describes the artifact rejection procedure.

claim: An automated procedure was implemented to reject trials in which at least one time point exceeded three interquartile ranges of all trial-specific values in both amplitude and gradient.
source: Prior to manual artefact rejection, an automated procedure was implemented to reject trials in which at least one time point exceeded three interquartile ranges of all trial-specific values in both amplitude and gradient (difference to previous time point).
evidence: This describes the automated artifact rejection procedure.

claim: Manual artefact rejection was conducted using FieldTrip's summary plot functions followed by trialwise artefact inspection.
source: Manual artefact rejection was conducted using FieldTrip's summary plot functions followed by trialwise artefact inspection.
evidence: This describes the manual artifact rejection procedure.

claim: Frequency decomposition of the data was achieved via Fourier analysis based on sliding time windows (moving forward in 10-ms increments).
source: After artefact rejection, frequency decomposition of the data was achieved via Fourier analysis based on sliding time windows (moving forward in 10-ms increments).
evidence: This describes the frequency decomposition method.

claim: The same pattern of results was observed when shortening the time windows, e.g. to four cycles of the lower frequencies and 200 ms for higher frequencies.
source: Note that the same pattern of results was observed when shortening the time windows, e.g. to four cycles of the lower frequencies and 200 ms for higher frequencies.
evidence: This demonstrates robustness of the findings to different time window parameters.

claim: The resulting power maps were normalised by dividing over the averaged −0.5 s prestimulus baseline window and subjected to direct comparison between conditions of interest.
source: The resulting power maps were normalised by dividing over the averaged −0.5 s prestimulus baseline window and subjected to direct comparison between conditions of interest.
evidence: This describes the normalization procedure for power maps.

claim: Recent rodent studies have demonstrated that memory reinstatement can be observed in highly localized cell assemblies in the hippocampus.
source: While this approach differs from other studies using spatial patterns across neocortical channels recorded via scalp EEG (Staudigl et al., 2015) or ECoG (Yaffe et al., 2014), recent rodent studies have demonstrated that – in the hippocampus – memory reinstatement can be observed in highly localized cell assemblies (Liu et al., 2012; Tayler et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to rodent studies.

claim: The field potential picked up by a single intracranial macro-electrode reflects contributions from all active cellular processes within the underlying volume of brain tissue (including synaptic activity, action potentials, fluctuations in glia etc.).
source: Moreover, as comprehensively reviewed by Buzsaki and colleagues (Buzsáki et al., 2012), the field potential picked up by a single intracranial macro-electrode reflects contributions from all active cellular processes within the underlying volume of brain tissue (including synaptic activity, action potentials, fluctuations in glia etc.).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a comprehensive review.

claim: Amplitude and frequency of the recorded field potential depend on the proportional contribution of multiple cellular sources.
source: As amplitude and frequency of the recorded field potential depend on the proportional contribution of these multiple sources, the time-frequency-decomposed signal might be particularly well suited to capture local hippocampal pattern completion processes in our study (i.e. firing patterns of distributed neurons bias the measured field potentials differentially; see also [Agarwal et al., 2014], although that study used even finer-grained micro-electrode field recordings from the rodent hippocampus).
evidence: This is a statement about the relationship between cellular activity and field potentials.
